en: The Mahāsannipāta-dharmaparyāya Sūtra, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Śīlaguṇabhadra, Imperially Appointed Court Honorable of the Third Rank, Acting Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments,
Great Master of the Transmission of the Dharma, and Purple-Robed Subject, by Imperial Decree.
Thus have I heard:
At one time, the Blessed One was traveling and arrived at the city of Pāṭaliputra, where he gathered together with a community of bhikṣus.

At that time, there was a faithful upāsaka in that city also named Pāṭaliputra, who had newly constructed a dwelling within the city. It was adorned in various ways, pure and spacious—a residence such as had never existed before, wherein śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others were to dwell.

At that time, the lay follower Mallika, hearing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was traveling through the region with a community of bhikṣus and had arrived there, felt great joy in his heart and immediately went to where the Buddha was.
Having arrived, he prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One; having paid homage, he stood to one side with palms joined and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I am a lay follower named Mallikā, and I have conceived pure faith in the World-Honored One."
"In this city of mine, I have newly constructed a dwelling that is pure and spacious; such a dwelling as this has never existed before, and śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others may dwell within it."
"I now invite the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus to dwell in my house; may the World-honored Buddha, out of compassion for me, accept my invitation.
At that time, the World-honored One accepted by remaining silent.

At that time, the upāsaka Mālikī, knowing that the Buddha had accepted his invitation by remaining silent, immediately prostrated with his head at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and departed from the assembly.
Returning to that house, he once again adorned it; throughout all the rooms and buildings, he sprinkled scented water everywhere upon the ground, making everything inside and out universally pure.

At that time, the lay follower Mallikā, having thus completed the construction and purification of her dwelling, returned to where the Buddha was. Upon arrival, she again prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and addressed him, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
The house I previously constructed has been entirely sprinkled with scented water, making both its interior and exterior pure.
I pray that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, together with the assembly of bhikṣus, will go to stay in that house; now is precisely the right time.
At that time, the World-Honored One, respectfully surrounded by a great assembly of bhikṣus, proceeded to the newly constructed residence of the upāsaka Māla.
Having arrived at that house, the Buddha first washed his feet and then entered it. Once inside, he surveyed the interior thoroughly on all sides and sat down calmly in the center of the hall.
The assembly of bhikṣus also each washed their feet and entered in succession; having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, they sat down in order behind the Buddha.

Later, the upāsaka Mālikī entered his residence, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and with palms joined in reverence, he paid homage to the entire assembly of bhikṣus; then, before the Buddha, he sat down to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, having comforted and exhorted the lay follower Mallika in various ways, immediately preached the essentials of the Dharma for him as was appropriate, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him.
At that time, the upāsaka Mālikī, having heard the Dharma, rejoiced and gave rise to pure faith.

Thus, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to that upāsaka as was appropriate, instructing, encouraging, benefiting, and gladdening him; as the night drew on, the Buddha addressed him, saying: "Mālikī!"
"When this night has passed, you shall know the time for yourself.

At that moment, having heard the Buddha's words, the lay follower Mālikā rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, and with palms joined in reverence, paid homage to the entire assembly of bhikṣus. He then circumambulated the Buddha three times and departed from the gathering.
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the lay follower Māṭhara had not long departed from the assembly, addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"These śrāvaka bhikṣus of mine have already abandoned sleep; they are all a pure assembly, free from worldly dust."
"If there are bhikṣus who delight in preaching the Dharma, they should preach it themselves as appropriate; they should not cease according to what is beneficial.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra received these instructions and remained there.

At that time, the World-Honored One folded his saṃghāṭī robe into four layers, sat upon the lion throne, and lay down on his right side in the auspicious and peaceful posture with one foot resting upon the other.

Not long after the Buddha had lain down to rest, at that time, in another place, there were certain non-Buddhist Nirgrantha Jñātiputras and others who harbored contempt and slander toward the Śrāvaka bhikṣus. Desiring to cause their destruction and incite conflict, they uttered unrighteous speech and various forms of abuse, saying:

"The Dharma known by me, those Śrāvakas are unable to comprehend; as for the Dharma they possess, I know it according to reality. Wrong practice belongs to you, while right practice belongs to me; what is beneficial belongs to me, while what is unbeneficial belongs to you. As for the Dharma you preach, if your former words are correct, your subsequent words are incorrect; if your subsequent words are correct, your former words are incorrect. You are unable to roar the great lion’s roar to preach the Dharma for the benefit of others."

At that time, when the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra and his followers sought to incite the causes and conditions for a vast dispute and uttered such words of disparagement, they looked at one another with expressions of cruel malice upon their faces.
He further spoke these words:

"The physical appearance and deportment of these śrāvaka bhikṣus lack tranquility; they are unable to abandon greed, have not attained liberation, cannot see the Dharma, and do not well know the path of transcendence. They cannot realize the noble fruits toward which they are directed, and the Dharma they practice was not taught by the Truly Perfectly Enlightened One."
Thus they uttered words of disparagement and incited strife.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra, having understood these matters, reflected to himself:
"The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has not been resting long; it would not be appropriate to inform the World-Honored One of such causes and conditions."
Having formed this thought, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"You should know that in another place there are certain non-Buddhist followers of Nirgrantha Jñātiputra and others who harbor contempt and slander toward the śrāvaka bhikṣus; they seek to cause division, incite strife, utter unrighteous speech, and revile them in various ways, saying: [The text continues with their specific criticisms.]...'"

"The dharmas that I know cannot be fully understood by the śrāvakas; those dharmas which they possess, I know them as they truly are. Wrong conduct is yours, right conduct is mine; what is beneficial is mine, what is unbeneficial is yours. As for the teachings you have spoken, if your former words were correct, your subsequent words are incorrect, or if your subsequent words are correct, your former words are incorrect; thus, you are unable to roar the great lion’s roar and teach the Dharma for the benefit of others."

"O Bhikṣus! When those Nirgrantha Jñātiputras and others, wishing to incite extensive causes for strife, uttered such words of disparagement, they looked at one another with faces of cruel malice and further said:

'The Śrāvaka bhikṣus lack the marks of physical excellence and dignified deportment; they are not tranquil, cannot abandon greed, have not attained liberation, do not perceive the Dharma, do not well know the path of transcendence, and have not realized the noble fruits toward which they are directed. The Dharma they practice was not spoken by the Truly and Fully Enlightened One.'"
"Having uttered such words of disparagement, they have incited strife and contention. O Bhikṣus!

You should now know that we, the great assembly of Śrāvakas, are all those whose minds are free from dust and pure; we have realized the various dharmas through direct perception, are well-versed in the path of deliverance, and each has already attained the noble fruit of realization."
The dharmas practiced by us śrāvakas are each and all personally proclaimed by the Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha; each is true and without falsehood.
"O Bhikṣus!

You should know that what the Buddha has proclaimed consists of the sūtras, geyas, vyākaraṇas, gāthās, itivṛttakas, jātakas, nidānas, vaipulyas, and adbhuta-dharmas. Such teachings as these, out of a heart of compassion, the Buddha has extensively proclaimed for the sake of sentient beings in accordance with reality, so that sentient beings may practice according to his instructions, cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya), and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to the world of devas and humans."
"Furthermore, monks, you should know that there is one dharma taught by the Buddha:
namely, that all sentient beings subsist by depending on nutriment; this is that one dharma."

The Buddha, out of a heart of compassion, extensively proclaimed these and other such teachings for the sake of sentient beings in accordance with reality, so that sentient beings might practice as taught, cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to the worlds of devas and humans.
"Furthermore, there are two dharmas taught by the Buddha:
namely, name and form.

Such dharmas as these were extensively and correctly proclaimed by the Buddha out of a heart of compassion for sentient beings, so that sentient beings might practice according to his teaching, cultivate the holy life, and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to the world of devas and humans."
"Furthermore, the three types of action were taught by the Buddha.
They are: first, bodily action; second, verbal action; and third, mental action.
These three types of action are further divided into two kinds: the wholesome and the unwholesome."
What is wholesome? It refers to wholesome conduct of bodily action, wholesome conduct of verbal action, and wholesome conduct of mental action.
What is called unwholesome?
That is to say: unwholesome conduct of bodily action, unwholesome conduct of verbal action, and unwholesome conduct of mental action.
"Furthermore, there are three unwholesome modes of reflection; these were taught by the Buddha."
These are called thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of harmfulness.
Furthermore, there are three wholesome thoughts taught by the Buddha:
thoughts of renunciation, thoughts of non-ill will, and thoughts of non-harmfulness.
"Furthermore, there are three unwholesome roots, as taught by the Buddha. They are:
the unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion."
"Furthermore, the three roots of goodness have been taught by the Buddha;
namely, the root of goodness of non-attachment, the root of goodness of non-hatred, and the root of goodness of non-delusion.
Furthermore, the three outflows have been taught by the Buddha."
That is to say: the outflow of sensual desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
Furthermore, there are three kinds of seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*) as taught by the Buddha:
namely, the seeking of sensual desire, the seeking of existence, and the seeking of the holy life (*brahmacarya-paryeṣaṇā*).
"Furthermore, there are three types of craving taught by the Buddha:
namely, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for form, and craving for the formless.
Furthermore, there are three realms taught by the Buddha."
That is to say, the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
Furthermore, the Buddha has spoken of three unwholesome realms:
the realm of lustful attachment, the realm of ill will, and the realm of harmful intent.
"Furthermore, the three wholesome realms have been taught by the Buddha;
namely, the realm of non-desire, the realm of non-hatred, and the realm of non-harming.
Furthermore, the three existences have been taught by the Buddha."
That is to say: existence in the desire realm, existence in the form realm, and existence in the formless realm.
"Furthermore, there are three groups as taught by the Buddha:
namely, the group of those fixed in error, the group of those fixed in correctness, and the group of those who are not fixed."
"Furthermore, there are three feelings taught by the Buddha:
namely, pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Furthermore, there are three sufferings taught by the Buddha."
That is to say: the suffering of saṃsāra, the suffering of suffering, and the suffering of change.
"Furthermore, there are three kinds of birth through desire, as taught by the Buddha:

namely, birth through desire in the Realm of Desire-dwelling (Kāmadhātu), birth through desire in the Realm of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati), and birth through desire in the Realm of Mastery over Others' Emanations (Paranirmitavaśavartin)."
"Furthermore, there are three kinds of birth in bliss, as taught by the Buddha.
There are beings who are born and, having been born, experience pleasure, such as a certain class among human beings; this is called the first birth in bliss.

Furthermore, there are beings who constantly experience joy and pleasure, a bliss that is vast, refreshing, and exhilarating, such as those in the Ābhāsvara Heaven; this is called the second birth in bliss."

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, for as long as they live, experience complete satisfaction in pleasure, like the gods of the Universal Purity Heaven; this is called the third birth in happiness.
Furthermore, the Buddha has taught that the accomplishment of the three types of meritorious deeds constitutes the practice of wisdom.

That is to say: the practice of wisdom perfected by the adornment of generosity, the practice of wisdom perfected by the adornment of ethical discipline, and the practice of wisdom perfected by the adornment of meditative concentration.
"Furthermore, there are three samādhis, as taught by the Buddha."
That is to say: the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra, the samādhi without vitarka and with only vicāra, and the samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra.
Furthermore, there are three other samādhis taught by the Buddha.
That is to say: the liberation-samādhi of emptiness, the liberation-samādhi of wishlessness, and the liberation-samādhi of signlessness.
"Furthermore, there are three abodes, as taught by the Buddha."
These are called the celestial abodes, the Brahma abodes, and the noble abodes.
Furthermore, there are three faculties taught by the Buddha:
namely, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has fully known."
"Furthermore, three types of supremacy were taught by the Buddha:
namely, supremacy in the world, supremacy in the Dharma, and supremacy in the self.
Furthermore, three types of Buddhas were taught by the Buddha."
That is to say: the Buddhas of the past, the Buddhas of the future, and the Buddhas of the present.
"Furthermore, there are three matters of verbal expression taught by the Buddha."
That is to say: the objects of discourse in the past, the objects of discourse in the future, and the objects of discourse in the present.
"Furthermore, there are three eyes; these were spoken by the Buddha."
That is to say: the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the wisdom eye.
Furthermore, there are the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) as taught by the Buddha:
the clear knowledge of the recollection of past lives, the clear knowledge of the arising and passing away of sentient beings, and the clear knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsrava*).
"Furthermore, the three supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are taught by the Buddha;
namely, the power of the psychic domain (*ṛddhi-vidhi*), the power of preaching the Dharma (*deśanā*), and the power of instruction (*anuśāsanī*).
Furthermore, the three impurities (*aśubha*) are taught by the Buddha."
That is to say: impurity of body, impurity of speech, and impurity of mind.
"Furthermore, there are three purities taught by the Buddha:
namely, purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind."
"Furthermore, the three trainings were taught by the Buddha;
namely, the training in ethical discipline, the training in concentration, and the training in wisdom.
Furthermore, the three categories were taught by the Buddha."
That is to say: the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of meditative concentration, and the aggregate of wisdom.
Furthermore, there are three fires as taught by the Buddha:
the fire of greed, the fire of hatred, and the fire of delusion.
"Furthermore, there are three stages taught by the Buddha:
the stage of birth, the stage of formation, and the stage of phenomena (*dharmāvasthā*).

Regarding such dharmas as these, the Buddha, out of a heart of compassion, extensively proclaimed them for the sake of sentient beings in accordance with reality, so that sentient beings might practice as taught, cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to the world of devas and humans."
"Furthermore, the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness is what has been taught by the Buddha.
That is to say: contemplating the impurity of the body, one does not give rise to [delusory] perceptions; one subdues ignorance and becomes detached from the sensations of affliction.
Contemplating sensation as suffering, contemplating the arising and ceasing of the mind, and skillfully contemplating all phenomena are likewise so."
"Furthermore, the four right efforts are taught by the Buddha. That is to say:
one arouses diligent effort, collects the mind and maintains mindfulness, to completely eliminate all unwholesome states that have already arisen;
and one arouses diligent effort, collects the mind and maintains mindfulness, to prevent all unwholesome states that have not yet arisen from arising."
For wholesome states that have not yet arisen, one arouses diligence and vigor, collects the mind and its resolve, and causes them to arise;
for wholesome states that have already arisen, one arouses diligence and vigor, collects the mind and its resolve, and causes them all to increase and reach fulfillment.
These are called the four right endeavors.
Furthermore, the four bases of psychic power were taught by the Buddha; they are: the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of intention accompanied by the formation of abandonment;

[the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of energy...; the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind...; and the basis of psychic power consisting of concentration of investigation accompanied by the formation of abandonment].
The base of psychic power consisting of concentration of energy and the cultivation of the formative forces of abandonment;
the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of mind and the cultivation of the formative forces of abandonment;
and the base of psychic power consisting of concentration of wisdom and the cultivation of the formative forces of abandonment.
"Furthermore, the four dhyānas have been taught by the Buddha. That is to say:

if a bhikṣu has already become detached from all sensual desires and unwholesome states, and possesses directed thought and sustained evaluation, this is called the first dhyāna, the concentration of joy and bliss born of seclusion.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu stills directed thought and sustained evaluation, with internal purity and one-pointedness of mind, being without directed thought or sustained evaluation, this is called the second dhyāna, the concentration of joy and bliss born of concentration."

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu is not attached to joy and dwells in the practice of equanimity, his body attains pliancy and sublime bliss; this is called the third absorption, the absorption of sublime bliss through the fading away of joy.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣu eliminates the perception of pleasure and likewise has no perception of pain, with neither mental elation nor mental distress, being without pain and without pleasure, this is called the fourth absorption, the absorption of pure mindfulness and equanimity.
These are called the four dhyānas.
Furthermore, the four immeasurables (apramāṇa) have been taught by the Buddha.

That is to say, if a bhikṣu arouses a mind of loving-kindness (maitrī), he first practices loving-kindness toward the eastern direction; he likewise practices loving-kindness toward the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below.
And that mind of loving-kindness is vast, immeasurable, and boundless in all places, all worlds, and all categories; it is also without limitation.
This is called immeasurable loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*).
The other three—compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*)—are likewise.
These are termed the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).
"Furthermore, the four formless absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti) are taught by the Buddha.

That is to say, if a bhikṣu, being detached from all forms, free from resistance and obstruction, and without mental application, contemplates infinite space—this mode of contemplation is called the absorption of the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana).

Furthermore, having transcended the sphere of space and no longer contemplating it, but contemplating only infinite consciousness—this mode of contemplation is called the absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana)."

Furthermore, transcending the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*), one does not observe that [sphere] either; rather, one observes that everything is non-existent. This mode of contemplation is called the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*).

Furthermore, transcending the mode of contemplation of the sphere of nothingness, it is called the meditative absorption of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*).
These are called the four formless attainments.
Furthermore, there are four knowledges taught by the Buddha:
namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
"Furthermore, there are four modes of abiding taught by the Buddha:
namely, abiding in all formations (*saṃskāra*), abiding in equanimity toward formations, abiding in tranquility toward formations, and abiding in wisdom regarding formations."
"Furthermore, the Four Noble Truths are taught by the Buddha;

namely, the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering."
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of pure giving as taught by the Buddha.
That is to say: there is giving where the giver is pure, but not the recipient;
or there is giving where the recipient is pure, but not the giver."
There may be giving where neither the giver nor the recipient exists, meaning the object given is pure;
there may be giving where both the giver and the recipient are pure.
"Furthermore, the four modes of birth were taught by the Buddha:
namely, birth from a womb, birth from an egg, birth from moisture, and miraculous birth.
Furthermore, the four matters concerning the mother's womb were taught by the Buddha."

That is to say: there is one who is able to fully cognize the process of entering the mother’s womb, the process of abiding in the mother’s womb, and the process of emerging from the mother’s womb; this is called the first matter regarding the womb.

There is one who is able to fully cognize the process of entering the mother’s womb and the process of abiding in the mother’s womb, but is unable to fully cognize the process of emerging from the mother’s womb; this is called the second matter regarding the womb.

There is one who is able to fully cognize the process of entering the mother’s womb, but is unable to fully cognize the process of abiding in the mother’s womb or the process of emerging from the mother’s womb; this is called the third matter regarding the womb.

There is that which cannot fully comprehend the matter of entering the mother’s womb, the matter of abiding in the mother’s womb, and the matter of emerging from the mother’s womb; this is called the fourth matter regarding the womb.
These and others like them are known as the four kinds of matters regarding the womb.
"Furthermore, the four stations of consciousness were taught by the Buddha. That is to say:
when form arises, with form as its condition, and abides in form, if it is accompanied by the expansive increase of the activity of delight, this is where consciousness dwells;
when feeling arises, with feeling as its condition, and abides in feeling, if it is accompanied by the expansive increase of the activity of delight, this is where consciousness dwells."
Perception arises, perception conditions, and perception abides; when joyful activity extensively increases, this is where consciousness dwells.
Volitional formations arise, volitional formations condition, and volitional formations abide; when joyful activity extensively increases, this is where consciousness dwells.
These and others like them are called the four stations of consciousness (*catasraḥ vijñānasthitayaḥ*).
"Furthermore, there are four dharma-phrases taught by the Buddha:

namely, the dharma-phrase of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the dharma-phrase of freedom from ill-will (*vyāpāda*), the dharma-phrase of equanimity (*samatā*), and the dharma-phrase of equanimous samādhi (*samata-samādhi*)."
"Furthermore, there are four *samannaphala* (results of the contemplative life) taught by the Buddha.
That is to say: if there is happiness in the present, this is a result of suffering;
if there is suffering in the present, this is a result of suffering."
If there is suffering in the present, this is a pleasant retribution;
if there is pleasure in the present, this is a pleasant retribution.
These are called the four *sāmaññaphala* (fruits of the ascetic life).
"Furthermore, the four paths are taught by the Buddha;
namely, non-patience, patience, subduing, and tranquility.
Furthermore, the four bases of supernormal power are taught by the Buddha."

That is to say: the supernormal power that is painful and slow, the supernormal power that is painful and swift, the supernormal power that is pleasant and slow, and the supernormal power that is pleasant and swift.
Furthermore, the four bodies of a stream-enterer are taught by the Buddha.

That is to say: there is a class of stream-enterers whose faith in the Buddha, the Tathāgata, is indestructible; who do not disparage śramaṇas, brahmins, devas, humans, Māras, or Brahmās; and who thoroughly understand worldly phenomena.

There is a class of stream-enterers whose minds have attained purity, who have realized the Buddha-dharma, and who, through right view and right conduct, each individually understands the dharma they themselves practice.
There is a class of stream-enterers whose hearts give rise to joy and delight, and who, upon seeing householders or those who have gone forth and maintain pure precepts, feel deep respect.

There is a class of stream-enterers who personally cultivate pure precepts, which they maintain in their entirety without impairment; their wisdom is clear and sharp, and their characteristics are well-composed and tranquil.
These and others like them are called the four types of stream-enterers.
"Furthermore, there are four fruits of the ascetic life, as taught by the Buddha:
namely, the fruit of stream-entry, the fruit of once-returning, the fruit of non-returning, and the fruit of arhatship."
"Furthermore, the four graspings were taught by the Buddha:
namely, the grasping for sensual pleasures, the grasping for views, the grasping for precepts and observances, and the grasping for the doctrine of self.
Furthermore, the four perceptions of meditative concentration were taught by the Buddha."
That is to say: when there is the turning toward the attainment of the practice of happiness through the dharma of vision, this is the perception of samādhi;
when there is the turning toward knowledge and vision, this is the perception of samādhi;
when there is the turning toward the discernment of wisdom, this is the perception of samādhi.
The transformation through which one who possesses a body attains the exhaustion of outflows—this is the perception of samādhi.
Furthermore, there are four powers taught by the Buddha:
namely, the power of wisdom, the power of diligence, the power of non-obstruction, and the power of gathering.
"Furthermore, there are four types of persons (pudgala) as taught by the Buddha. There is the person who thinks:

'I am the one who practices, I am the one who maintains the precepts, and I am the one who accords with the Dharma; it is not another who practices, it is not another who maintains the precepts, and it is not another who accords with the Dharma.

There is the person who thinks: 'It is another who practices, another who maintains the precepts, and another who accords with the Dharma; it is not I who practice, it is not I who maintain the precepts, and it is not I who accord with the Dharma.'"

There is a person who thinks: "I am able to practice, and others are also able to practice; I maintain the precepts, and others also maintain the precepts; I am in accordance with the Dharma, and others are also in accordance with the Dharma.

There is another person who thinks: "I am not able to practice, and others are also not able to practice; I do not maintain the precepts, and others also do not maintain the precepts; I am not in accordance with the Dharma, and others are also not in accordance with the Dharma."
These and others like them are called the four types of *pudgala*.
Furthermore, there are four matters concerning the community (*saṃgha*) taught by the Buddha:
namely, dwelling together with the community, eating and drinking together with the community, performing confession together with the community, and sharing resources together with the community.
"Furthermore, there are four wheels taught by the Buddha:
namely, the excellent exposition of the sublime Dharma, reliance upon a true person, an impartial mind of aspiration, and the prior cultivation of wisdom."
"Furthermore, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) are taught by the Buddha;
namely, generosity, pleasant speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.
Furthermore, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are taught by the Buddha."

That is to say: the analytical knowledge of meaning (artha-pratisaṃvid), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dharma-pratisaṃvid), the analytical knowledge of eloquence (pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid), and the analytical knowledge of expression (nirukti-pratisaṃvid).
Furthermore, there are four afflictions as taught by the Buddha.
That is to say: the affliction of desire, the affliction of existence, the affliction of views, and the affliction of ignorance.
"Furthermore, there are four modes of practice taught by the Buddha."
That is to say: the formations of desire, the formations of existence, the formations of views, and the formations of ignorance.
Furthermore, there are four aggregates of the body as taught by the Buddha:
namely, the aggregate of ignorance, the aggregate of hatred, the aggregate of attachment to precepts and observances, and the aggregate of all attachments.
"Furthermore, the Buddha has taught that there are four ways in which craving arises.
That is to say, there may be a bhikṣu who, because of his robes, gives rise to craving; because craving arises, he immediately gives rise to grasping and attachment."
There is a bhikṣu who, because of food and drink, gives rise to a mind of attachment; because this mind of attachment arises, he immediately gives rise to grasping and clinging.
There is a bhikṣu who, because of bedding and seating, gives rise to a mind of attachment; because this mind of attachment arises, he immediately gives rise to grasping and clinging.
There is a bhikṣu who, due to various objects of enjoyment, gives rise to craving; because craving arises, he immediately gives rise to grasping.
This is called the four ways in which craving arises.
"Furthermore, there are four nutriments taught by the Buddha:
namely, edible food, contact as nutriment, volition as nutriment, and consciousness as nutriment.
Furthermore, there are four things that need not be guarded against, as taught by the Buddha."
That is to say, the Tathāgata does not need to guard his bodily actions, for his body is free from all faults;
the Tathāgata does not need to guard his verbal actions, for his speech is free from all faults;
the Tathāgata does not need to guard his mental actions, for his mind is free from all faults.
The Tathāgata does not guard his life-span, for his life is subject to no diminution.
"Furthermore, the four inversions were taught by the Buddha:
namely, to regard the impermanent as permanent; therefore, there arise the inversion of perception, the inversion of mind, and the inversion of view."
Taking what is suffering to be pleasure, one thus gives rise to perversion of perception, mind, and view.
Taking what is non-self to be self, one thus gives rise to perversion of perception, mind, and view.
To regard the impure as pure gives rise to distortions of perception, mind, and view.
These and others like them are called the four perversions (*catur-viparyāsa*).
Furthermore, there are four types of unwholesome speech, as taught by the Buddha.
That is to say: false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech.
"Furthermore, there are four kinds of wholesome speech taught by the Buddha:
namely, truthful speech, straightforward speech, non-divisive speech, and speech in accordance with the Dharma."
"Furthermore, there are four non-ārya practices taught by the Buddha:
claiming to have seen what one has not seen, claiming to have heard what one has not heard, claiming to remember what one has lost mindfulness of, and claiming to know what one does not know."
"Furthermore, there are four modes of conduct (*āryavṛtta*) taught by the Buddha:
namely, to say one has seen what was truly seen, to say one has heard what was truly heard, to say one has recollected what was truly recollected, and to say one has known what was truly known."
"Furthermore, there are four ways of answering questions as taught by the Buddha:
the categorical answer, the analytical answer, the answer by counter-question, and the answer by remaining silent.

Such teachings were extensively proclaimed by the Buddha out of a heart of compassion for the sake of sentient beings, according to the truth, so that sentient beings might practice as instructed, cultivate the holy life, and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to the world of devas and humans."
The Scripture on the Dharma-Door of the Great Assembly Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Upper;
The Scripture on the Dharma-Door of the Great Assembly Spoken by the Buddha, Volume Lower.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Imperial Meritorious Servant, Acting Director of the Court of Imperial Entertainments.
The Dharma Master of the State, the Purple-Robed Subject Shi Hu, respectfully translates by imperial decree:
"Furthermore, O Bhikṣus!
You should know that the five aggregates of clinging are what the Buddha has taught."

That is to say: the aggregate of clinging to form, the aggregate of clinging to feeling, the aggregate of clinging to perception, the aggregate of clinging to formations, and the aggregate of clinging to consciousness.
Furthermore, there are the five sensual desires, as taught by the Buddha.
That is to say: when the eye sees forms, the mind feels joy and desire; with a mind of joy and desire, it grasps and clings to the objects of form.
It is the same for the ear hearing sounds, the nose smelling odors, the tongue discerning tastes, and the body feeling tangibles.
"Furthermore, there are five hindrances taught by the Buddha:
namely, the hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt."
"Furthermore, there are five kinds of fetters that are constituent parts of the afflictions (*kleśa*), as taught by the Buddha. Namely:

the fetter of the constituent part of desire-attachment (*kāmarāga*), the fetter of the constituent part of ill-will (*vyāpāda*), the fetter of the constituent part of the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the fetter of the constituent part of adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and the fetter of the constituent part of doubt (*vicikitsā*)."
"Furthermore, there are five kinds of stinginess taught by the Buddha:
stinginess regarding food and drink, stinginess regarding virtuous deeds, stinginess regarding gain and offerings, stinginess regarding physical appearance, and stinginess regarding the Dharma."
"Furthermore, there are five faculties of feeling (*vedanendriya*) as taught by the Buddha:
namely, the faculty of pleasant feeling, the faculty of painful feeling, the faculty of joyful feeling, the faculty of sorrowful feeling, and the faculty of equanimous feeling."
"Furthermore, there are five supreme faculties taught by the Buddha:
namely, the faculty of faith, the faculty of diligence, the faculty of mindfulness, the faculty of concentration, and the faculty of wisdom."
"Furthermore, the five powers are taught by the Buddha;
namely, the power of faith, the power of diligence, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom.
Furthermore, the five powers of training are taught by the Buddha."
That is to say: the power of training in faith, the power of training in diligence, the power of training in mindfulness, the power of training in concentration, and the power of training in wisdom.
Furthermore, there are five elements of renunciation, as taught by the Buddha.

It is said that there may be a bhikṣu who, though possessed of great learning, cannot see suffering; his mind remains receptive to it, and he has not yet attained freedom from desire. Following various objects of desire, he gives rise to a longing for them, neither withdrawing nor sinking away, and thus fails to achieve liberation.

Yet, by means of this very condition, he later becomes able to contemplate all objects of desire and gives rise to a mind free from desire. His longing for desire withdraws and sinks away; he delights in liberation, practices correctly, and attains liberation of mind.
Once liberation of mind arises, he is then able to distance himself from discordant dharmas and abide in a mind free from desire.
For this reason, by taking desire as a condition, one brings forth the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).

There may be a bhikṣu who is possessed of great learning, yet he is unable to see suffering; his mind remains receptive to it, and being unable to abandon hatred, he gives rise to a mind of anger toward obstructive objects. He does not retreat, nor does he sink away, and he has not yet attained liberation.

By means of this very condition, he later becomes able to contemplate those obstructive objects again and gives rise to a mind free from hatred. His hateful mind recedes and vanishes; he comes to delight in liberation, practices the correct conduct well, and attains liberation of mind.
When the mind of liberation arises, one is then able to distance oneself from discordant factors and abide in a mind free from hatred.
For this reason, with hatred as a condition, the outflow-free state is induced.

There may be a bhikṣu who is possessed of great learning, yet he is unable to see suffering; his mind remains receptive to it, and he has not yet abandoned harmful intent. Toward objects that are disagreeable to the mind, he gives rise to a harmful thought, neither withdrawing nor sinking [from it], and thus fails to attain liberation.

By means of this very condition, he later becomes able to contemplate those same disagreeable objects and gives rise to a non-harming mind. His harmful mind withdraws and sinks away; he delights in liberation, practices correctly, and attains liberation of the mind.
Once the liberated mind arises, he is then able to distance himself from discordant factors and abide in a state of non-harming mind.
For this reason, by taking harm as a condition, one brings forth the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*).

Suppose there is a bhikṣu who is widely learned, yet he is unable to see suffering; his mind remains receptive [to defilements], and not having abandoned the marks of form (*rūpa-nimitta*), he gives rise to a mind attached to various forms, neither withdrawing nor sinking [from them], and thus has not yet attained liberation.

By means of this very condition, he later becomes able to contemplate those objective spheres of form and give rise to a mind detached from form; his mind of attachment to form withdraws and sinks away, and through delighting in liberation and practicing correctly, he attains liberation of mind (*cetovimukti*).
When the mind of liberation arises, one is then able to distance oneself from discordant factors and abide in a state of detachment from form and mind.
For this reason, by taking form as a condition, the outflow-free state is induced.

There may be a bhikṣu who, though possessing great learning, is unable to see suffering; he clings to the existence of a body and has not yet abandoned the perception of a body. Regarding this body, he gives rise to the notion that it truly exists, neither regressing nor sinking [from it], and thus remains unable to attain liberation.

By means of this very condition, he later becomes able to contemplate the cessation of the body, giving rise to the perception of the body’s cessation. His mind regresses from clinging and he comes to delight in liberation. Skillfully performing right practice, he attains liberation of mind;
once liberation of mind arises, he is then able to distance himself from discordant dharmas and abide in the perception of the body’s cessation.
For this reason, with the body as a condition, one draws forth the outflow-free [state].
Such categories as these are called the five realms of renunciation (*pañca-niḥsaraṇa-dhātavaḥ*).
Furthermore, the five bases of liberation (*pañca-vimukti-sthānāni*) were taught by the Buddha.

It refers to a bhikṣu who approaches and serves a Dharma teacher, honoring and respecting him, practicing the holy life without even a moment’s rest; through such approach and service, he immediately gains benefit.

When he hears the teacher proclaim the true Dharma, his heart gives rise to joy and delight, conceiving a profound sense of the Dharma. Following the arising of that mind, although he is not yet able to extensively hear, receive, and remember it, he is able to know a single dharma therein. As he knows that one dharma, he understands its meaning. If he did not understand its meaning, he would be unable to give rise to a joyful mind toward the Dharma.

Therefore, having understood its meaning, joy arises in the mind; because the mind is joyful, the body attains pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); through bodily pliancy, one experiences pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*); because of that pleasant feeling, the mind abides in meditative equipoise (*samāhita*).

Abiding in that state of mind, one is able to know things as they truly are and contemplate them as they truly are. By contemplating them as they truly are, one becomes detached from dust and free from craving, attaining the knowledge of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna*).

When the knowledge of liberation arises, one realizes: "Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."

There is a bhikṣu who, in the presence of a Dharma-preacher, attends upon and serves him with respect and reverence, practicing the holy life without ceasing for even a moment. As he attends upon and serves him, he hears the Dharma;
as he hears it, his heart gives rise to joy and delight, conceiving a profound sense of the Dharma.

Following the arising of that mind, he is able to hear and receive it extensively and remember it extensively. As he understands the various dharmas, he immediately comprehends their meanings; if he did not comprehend their meanings, he would be unable to give rise to a joyful heart toward the Dharma.

Therefore, having understood all meanings, joy arises in the mind; because of this joyful mind, the body attains pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); through bodily pliancy, one experiences pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*); because of pleasant feeling, the mind abides in meditative equipoise (*samāhita*).

Abiding in that state of mind, one is able to know things as they truly are and contemplate them as they truly are; by contemplating them as they truly are, one becomes detached from dust and free from craving, attaining the knowledge of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna*).

When the knowledge of liberation arises, one realizes: "Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."

There is a bhikṣu who, in the presence of a Dharma teacher, draws near and serves him, honoring and revering him as he cultivates the holy life without ceasing for even a moment. In accordance with his drawing near and service, he hears the Dharma;

in accordance with what he hears, joy and happiness arise in his mind, and he conceives a profound sense of the Dharma. Following the arising of that mind, he is able to listen extensively, receive, and retain it, and furthermore, he is able to understand each and every meaning exactly as it is. He then explains and expounds these meanings in detail for others. If he did not understand these meanings, he would be unable to give rise to a heart of joy toward the Dharma.

Therefore, having understood all meanings, joy arises in the mind; because the mind is joyful, the body attains pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); through bodily pliancy, one is conjoined with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*); because of pleasant feeling, the mind abides in meditative equipoise (*samāhita*);

by abiding in that state of mind, one is able to know things as they truly are and contemplate them as they truly are; through such true contemplation, one becomes detached from dust and free from craving, attaining the knowledge of liberation;

once the knowledge of liberation has arisen, one realizes: "Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
There is a bhikṣu who, in the presence of a Dharma-preacher, draws near and serves him, honoring and respecting him, practicing the holy life without even a moment’s interruption.

In accordance with his drawing near and service, he immediately hears the Dharma; in accordance with what he hears, joy arises in his mind, and he conceives a profound sense of the Dharma. Following the arising of that mind, he is able to listen extensively, receive, and remember it, and furthermore, his mind can abide in a single object, neither regressing nor sinking.

Regarding the Dharma he has heard, through successive investigation and analysis, he gives rise to right wisdom; following the arising of investigation and analysis, he understands each and every phenomenon; following his understanding of the phenomena, he comprehends their meanings and explains them in detail for others. If he did not comprehend the meanings, he would be unable to give rise to a joyful mind toward the Dharma.

Therefore, having understood all meanings, joy arises in the mind; because the mind is joyful, the body attains pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); through bodily pliancy, one is associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*); because of pleasant feeling, the mind abides in meditative equipoise (*samāhita*);

by abiding in that state of mind, one is able to know things as they truly are and contemplate them as they truly are; through such contemplation as it truly is, one becomes detached from dust and free from craving, attaining the knowledge of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna*);

once the knowledge of liberation has arisen, one realizes: "Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."

There is a bhikṣu who, in the presence of a Dharma-preacher, draws near and serves him, honoring and respecting him, practicing the holy life without even a moment's rest; as he draws near and serves him, he immediately hears the Dharma.

According to what they hear, their minds give rise to joy and delight, conceiving a profound thought of the Dharma. Following the arising of that mind, they are able to extensively listen, receive, and remember; their minds abide in a single object, neither regressing nor sinking. Regarding the Dharma they have heard, they engage in investigation and analysis, giving rise to right wisdom. Having done so, they are further able to skillfully dwell with a concentrated mind within various gateways of samādhi. As the mind dwells thus, it becomes increasingly superior, whereby they clearly understand each and every phenomenon. Following this understanding of phenomena, they comprehend their meanings and extensively analyze and expound them for others. If they do not comprehend these meanings, they will be unable to give rise to a heart of joy toward the Dharma.

Therefore, having understood all meanings, joy arises in the mind; because the mind is joyful, the body attains pliancy (*praśrabdhi*); through bodily pliancy, one is associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*); because of pleasant feeling, the mind abides in *samāhita*;

by abiding in that state of mind, one is able to know things as they truly are (*yathābhūtam*) and contemplate them as they truly are; through such contemplation, one becomes detached from dust and free from craving, attaining the knowledge of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna*);

once the knowledge of liberation has arisen, one realizes: "Birth for me has been exhausted, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
These are called the five bases of liberation.
Furthermore, there are the five destinies spoken of by the Buddha:
namely, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and devas.
"Furthermore, the five Pure Abodes are what the Buddha has taught;
namely, Avṛha, Atapa, Sudarśana, Sudṛśa, and Akaniṣṭha."
"Furthermore, there are five ways of entering for a person, as taught by the Buddha. These are:
entry into the intermediate state, entry into rebirth, entry with exertion, entry without exertion, and entry into the higher stream. These are called the five ways of entering for a person."

Regarding such dharmas as these, out of a heart of compassion, the Buddha extensively proclaimed them for the sake of sentient beings in accordance with reality, so that sentient beings might practice as taught, cultivate the holy life, and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to the world of devas and humans.
"Furthermore, the six internal bases were taught by the Buddha;
namely, the eye base, the ear base, the nose base, the tongue base, the body base, and the mind base."
"Furthermore, the six external bases were taught by the Buddha;
namely, the base of forms, the base of sounds, the base of odors, the base of tastes, the base of tangibles, and the base of mental phenomena."
"Furthermore, the six consciousnesses are taught by the Buddha;
namely, eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness."
"Furthermore, there are six types of contact, as taught by the Buddha:
namely, eye-contact, ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, and mind-contact."
"Furthermore, there are six feelings, as taught by the Buddha.

They are: all feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; all feelings produced with ear-contact as condition; all feelings produced with nose-contact as condition; all feelings produced with tongue-contact as condition; all feelings produced with body-contact as condition; and all feelings produced with mind-contact as condition."
"Furthermore, there are six perceptions taught by the Buddha:
namely, perception of forms, perception of sounds, perception of odors, perception of tastes, perception of tangibles, and perception of mental phenomena."
"Furthermore, there are six kinds of craving taught by the Buddha:
namely, craving for forms, craving for sounds, craving for odors, craving for tastes, craving for tangibles, and craving for mental phenomena."
"Furthermore, there are six bases of delight taught by the Buddha.
Namely: seeing a pleasing form is a base of delight;
hearing a pleasing sound is a base of delight;..."
Smelling pleasant fragrances is a source of delight;
perceiving pleasant tastes is a source of delight;
experiencing pleasant tactile sensations is a source of delight.
The discernment of wholesome dharmas is a source of mental delight.
Furthermore, the Buddha has taught six sources of mental displeasure:
namely, seeing an unlovely form is a source of mental displeasure;
Hearing unpleasant sounds is a source of dissatisfaction;
smelling unpleasant odors is a source of dissatisfaction;
perceiving unpleasant tastes is a source of dissatisfaction.
"To perceive a touch that is unlovely is a ground for displeasure;
to discriminate unwholesome phenomena is a ground for displeasure.
Furthermore, there are six modes of equanimity, as taught by the Buddha."

That is to say: the activity of seeing forms is the relinquishing of forms; the activity of hearing sounds is the relinquishing of sounds; the activity of smelling odors is the relinquishing of odors; the activity of discerning tastes is the relinquishing of tastes; the activity of feeling tangibles is the relinquishing of tangibles; and the activity of cognizing phenomena is the relinquishing of phenomena.
"Furthermore, there are six recollections taught by the Buddha:
namely, recollection of the Buddha, recollection of the Dharma, recollection of the Sangha, recollection of ethical discipline, recollection of generosity, and recollection of the devas."
"Furthermore, there are six practices taught by the Buddha:
namely, the practice of seeing, the practice of hearing, the practice of benefiting others, the practice of training, the practice of discernment, and the practice of mindfulness."
"Furthermore, there are six dharmas free from defilement taught by the Buddha.
That is to say: if a bhikṣu currently abides in compassionate action of body, all the holy life (brahmacarya) he has practiced from the beginning remains firm and unbroken;
if a bhikṣu currently abides in compassionate action of speech, all the holy life he has practiced from the beginning remains firm and unbroken."
There is a bhikṣu who dwells in the present with a mental action of loving-kindness; from the beginning he has practiced the holy life (brahmacarya), which is firm and indestructible.

There is a bhikṣu who receives gains in accordance with the Dharma and begs for alms in accordance with the Dharma; whatever he obtains, he eats in accordance with the Dharma, maintaining his own practice and remaining far removed from what is contrary to the Dharma; from the beginning he has practiced the holy life, which is firm and indestructible.

There is a bhikṣu who cultivates the practice of pure precepts—unbroken, unimpaired, and free from all faults; he increases the power of the wholesome, and in all his conduct, his preceptual practice is complete; from the beginning he has practiced the holy life, which is firm and indestructible.

There is a bhikṣu who does not cling to the view of a self-identity, conceives of renunciation, and seeks the exhaustion of suffering; in accordance with all his practices, he does not abide in any views, and from the very beginning, the holy life he cultivates remains firm and unbroken.
These and others like them are called the six dharmas of detachment from dust.
Furthermore, the Buddha has taught that there are six roots of strife.

That is to say, there is a certain class of *pudgala* who delights in committing offenses themselves, delights in associating with those who commit offenses, and constantly desires that others hold them in affection and respect.

There is a class of persons who delight in committing offenses themselves and also delight in associating with those who commit offenses; they constantly desire that others love and respect them, yet they do not revere the Buddha, do not revere the Dharma, and are unable to contemplate the Dharma.

There is another class of persons who delight in committing offenses themselves and also delight in associating with those who commit offenses; they constantly desire that others love and respect them, and furthermore, they delight in quarreling and disputing with the Saṃgha.

There is yet another class of persons who possess various secondary afflictions such as flattery, deception, stinginess, envy, and concealment, as well as the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), wrong views, extreme views, and the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which they are unable to abandon.

There is a class of persons who possess the view of a self-identity and give rise to perverted thoughts; furthermore, they do not revere the Buddha, do not revere the Dharma, and are unable to contemplate the Dharma.
There is another class of persons who possess the view of a self-identity and give rise to perverted thoughts; furthermore, they constantly delight in quarreling with the Saṃgha.
These are called the six roots of contention.
Furthermore, there are six kinds of remedial means for transcendence taught by the Buddha.
That is to say, there is a bhikṣu who speaks as follows:

"I cultivate the contemplation of the liberation of the mind through loving-kindness; whatever actions I perform, I know them all as they truly are. By initiating diligence and the counteractive force of a loving mind, I am able to completely exhaust all thoughts of hatred."
"Because one contemplates liberation through such a mind of loving-kindness, there is no room for any ill-will to be admitted.
One simply contemplates that this loving-kindness is present before one; therefore, ill-will has no basis from which to arise."
Why is this? Because that mind of loving-kindness is the cause for renunciation.
There was a bhikṣu who spoke as follows:

"I cultivate the liberation through the contemplation of compassion; whatever actions I perform, I know them all as they truly are. By initiating the antidote of diligent compassion, I am able to completely exhaust all thoughts of malice."
"Because of such liberation through the contemplation of compassion, there is no room for any harmful intent to be admitted.
Thus, by merely contemplating that compassion is present before one, harmful intent has no basis from which to arise.
Why is this? Because that compassionate mind is the cause for renunciation.
There was a bhikṣu who spoke as follows:

"I cultivate the liberation through the mind of joy; I know, as it truly is, whatever actions are performed, and I initiate the joyful mind of diligence as an antidote, whereby I am able to completely exhaust all states of non-joyful mind."
"By means of observing this liberation of the mind through joy, there is no room for any lack of joy to be admitted.
Thus, one observes only that joy is present before one; therefore, a lack of joy does not arise in this state.
Why is this? Because that mind of joy is the cause for renunciation.
There is a bhikṣu who speaks as follows:

"I cultivate the contemplation of the liberation of the mind through equanimity; whatever actions I perform, I know them all as they truly are. I arouse diligence as an antidote to the mind of equanimity, whereby I am able to completely exhaust the mind of sensual desire."
"Because one contemplates liberation through such a mind of equanimity, there is no room for any mind of sensual desire to find a place to abide.
Thus, by contemplating only that mind of equanimity as it manifests before them, the mind of sensual desire does not arise in that state.
Why is this? Because that mind of relinquishment is the cause for renunciation.
There was a bhikṣu who spoke as follows:

"I cultivate the contemplation of the signless liberation of mind; whatever actions I perform, I know them all as they truly are. I arouse diligence through the counteractive measure of the signless mind, whereby I am able to completely exhaust all minds that grasp at signs."
"Because of this contemplation of the signless liberation of the mind, there is no room for any mind that grasps at signs to find a place to abide.
Thus, one contemplates only that signless mind manifesting before one; therefore, a mind that grasps at signs does not arise in this state.
Why is this? Because it is the cause for the mind to emerge from signlessness.
There is a bhikṣu who speaks as follows:
"I cultivate resolute practice and employ the dharma of resolution as an antidote; thus, I am able to completely exhaust all doubt and hesitation.
Because of such resolute practice, there is no room for any doubt or hesitation to remain."
Rather, one simply observes that resolute mind manifesting before them; therefore, no doubt or hesitation arises in this state. Why is this?
Because these constitute the causes for the definitive emergence of the mind,
such factors as these are called the six kinds of remedial realms of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇadhātu*).
Out of a heart of compassion, the Buddha extensively taught these dharmas to sentient beings in accordance with reality.
"And thus cause sentient beings to practice as taught, to cultivate the various holy conducts (brahmacarya), and to bring benefit, peace, and happiness to the world of devas and humans.
Furthermore, the seven factors of enlightenment (saptabodhyanga) are what the Buddha has taught."

That is to say: the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of rapture, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.
"Furthermore, there are seven objects of concentration taught by the Buddha:
namely, right observation, right deliberation, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right exertion, and right mindfulness."
"Furthermore, there are seven contemplations of liberation taught by the Buddha. They are:

the contemplation of impurity, the contemplation of death, the contemplation of non-attachment to food, the contemplation of the lack of delight in all worldly realms, the contemplation of impermanence, the contemplation of suffering in impermanence, and the contemplation of the boundlessness of suffering."
"Furthermore, there are seven powers taught by the Buddha:
namely, the power of faith, the power of mindfulness, the power of fearlessness, the power of diligence, the power of patience, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom."
"Furthermore, there are seven types of individuals (pudgala) taught by the Buddha. Namely:
one liberated by mind, one liberated both ways, one liberated by wisdom, a bodily witness, one liberated through faith, a practitioner by dharma, and a practitioner by faith."
"Furthermore, the seven stations of consciousness were taught by the Buddha. These are:
first, various bodies and various perceptions—namely, the humans and devas of the desire realm, which are stations of consciousness;
second, various bodies and a single perception—namely, the devas of the first dhyāna, which are stations of consciousness;"
The realm of various perceptions within a single body refers to the Second Dhyāna Heaven, which is where consciousness dwells;
the realm of a single perception within a single body refers to the Third Dhyāna Heaven, which is where consciousness dwells;
and the Sphere of Infinite Space is also where consciousness dwells.
The gods of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness are where consciousness dwells;
the gods of the Sphere of Nothingness are where consciousness dwells.
These are called the seven stations of consciousness.

With a heart of compassion, the Buddha has extensively proclaimed these and other such teachings for the sake of sentient beings in accordance with reality, so that sentient beings may practice as taught, cultivate the holy life, and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to the worlds of devas and humans.
"Furthermore, the eight liberations have been taught by the Buddha. They are: the liberation of one who perceives internal forms while observing external forms;

the liberation of one who has no perception of internal forms while observing external forms; the liberation of the beautiful, attained through dwelling in its perfection; the liberation of the sphere of infinite space; the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness; the liberation of the sphere of nothingness; the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling."
"Furthermore, the eight bases of mastery (aṣṭau abhibhvāyatanāni) are taught by the Buddha. That is to say:

when one possesses the perception of internal forms and observes external forms that are limited, and while performing this observation gives rise to superior knowledge and vision, this is called a base of mastery;

when one possesses the perception of internal forms and observes external forms that are manifold, and while performing this observation gives rise to superior knowledge and vision, this is called a base of mastery."

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as limited; when performing this contemplation, one gives rise to superior knowledge and vision—this is a *abhibhvāyatana* (sphere of mastery).
Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as vast; when performing this contemplation, one gives rise to superior knowledge and vision—this is a *abhibhvāyatana*.

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as blue—namely, contemplating them like an *umakā* flower or blue cloth; within these two types of blue, they are all manifest as blue, appear as blue, and emit blue light, being extensive, abundant, and pure. When performing this contemplation, one gives rise to superior knowledge and vision—this is a *abhibhvāyatana*.

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as yellow—namely, like the *kṛṣṇāgāra* flower or a yellow garment. Within these two types of yellow, they all manifest as yellow, appear as yellow, and radiate yellow light; being vast, abundant, and pure, when one performs this contemplation and gives rise to superior knowledge and vision, this is a "sphere of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as red—namely, like the *pāṇḍu-ujjvaka* flower or a red garment. Within these two types of red, they all manifest as red, appear as red, and radiate red light; being vast, abundant, and pure, when one performs this contemplation and gives rise to superior knowledge and vision, this is a "sphere of mastery."

Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms as white—namely, observing them like white flowers or white garments. Within these two aspects of whiteness, they are all white, manifesting as white, emitting white light, vast, abundant, and pure. When one performs this contemplation and gives rise to superior knowledge and vision, this is called a "sphere of mastery" (abhibhvāyatana).
These and others like them are called the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
Furthermore, there are eight worldly conditions (*lokadharma*) taught by the Buddha:
namely, gain and loss, defamation and praise, fame and insignificance, suffering and pleasure.
"Furthermore, the Eightfold Noble Path is what has been taught by the Buddha.
That is to say: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."
This is called the Eightfold Noble Path.

Such teachings as these, out of a heart of compassion, the Buddha has extensively proclaimed for the sake of sentient beings in accordance with reality, so that sentient beings may practice as taught, cultivate the holy life, and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to the world of devas and humans.
"Furthermore, there are nine abodes of sentient beings, as taught by the Buddha.
These are: first, those with diverse bodies and diverse perceptions, namely the humans and devas of the desire realm;
second, those with diverse bodies and a single perception, namely the devas of the first dhyāna;..."
The realm of sentient beings where there is a single body with diverse perceptions refers to the Second Dhyāna Heaven;
the realm of sentient beings where there is a single body with a single perception refers to the Third Dhyāna Heaven;
and the realm of sentient beings where there is the sphere of infinite space.
The Heaven of Infinite Consciousness is an abode of sentient beings;
the Heaven of Nothingness is an abode of sentient beings;
the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception is an abode of sentient beings.
And the Heaven of Non-conception—these are the abodes of sentient beings.
These are called the nine abodes of sentient beings.

Such dharmas as these, out of a heart of compassion, the Buddha has extensively proclaimed for the sake of sentient beings in accordance with reality, so that sentient beings may practice them as taught, cultivate the holy life, and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to the world of devas and humans.
"Furthermore, there are ten practices of fulfillment taught by the Buddha. They are:

unshakable right view, unshakable right intention, unshakable right speech, unshakable right action, unshakable right livelihood, unshakable right effort, unshakable right patience, unshakable right concentration, unshakable right liberation, and unshakable right knowledge."

These are called the ten practices of fulfillment. Such dharmas as these were extensively proclaimed by the Buddha out of his compassionate heart for the sake of sentient beings, in accordance with reality, so that sentient beings might practice as taught, cultivate the holy life, and bring benefit, peace, and happiness to the world of devas and humans.

At that time, the Blessed One, knowing that the Venerable Śāriputra had preached the Dharma to the bhikṣus as was appropriate for them, rose calmly from his reclining posture and addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"Excellent!"
Excellent, Śāriputra!
What you have spoken is indeed what the Buddha has taught.
This teaching is named the "Dharma Gate of the Great Assembly. In the future final age, it will be able to bring great benefit to sentient beings.
In that future final age, my bhikṣus who practice the holy life should receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and disseminate this Dharma Gate of the Great Assembly.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

In the final age, if there is a person who attains and upholds this Dharma-gate of the Great Assembly, that person, among the teachings of all future Buddhas, will be a son of noble family with pure faith; they will develop deep love and joy for the Buddha’s teachings, gaining vast understanding and great rejoicing in their heart.
At that time, having heard the Buddha praise this Dharma-gate of the Great Assembly, the bhikṣus rejoiced, accepted it with faith, prostrated to the Buddha, and withdrew.
*The Sūtra of the Dharma-gate of the Great Assembly*, Scroll Lower.
